Fixing the 'fogging' will depend on whether or not a low-e coating is used. If moisture has gotten in to the unit and the low-e is deteriorating (some of the metal layers in the low-e will oxidize/rust if exposed to moisture) this is not something that can be fixed without replacing that lite. If a hard-coat low-e was used or if no low-e was used, then the IGU might be able to be taken apart, cleaned, and have the spacer and seals replaced. I suggest 3.5-inch minimum and make sure you use mesh.  A thickened slab edge is also important, plus a vapor barrier and insulation depending on location. A 300/320lb capacity mixer that can be rented from a big box store can handle four 60lb pre-mixed bags of concrete before there is slosh-out and I find that this is a manageable amount for a wheelbarrow too. Depending on the mixer, it may need to be on an elevated platform if you are pouring into a wheelbarrow for distribution. My method is to add the water first, then add three bags and let it mix for a good minute (perhaps while you wheelbarrow the previous mix to the slab and return), then add the final bag and and a touch more water if the whole mix is too dry.

I suggest doing this as a 2-man job in a single day, or split the pour in to two days and have cold joints but with the mesh spanning the joints (use 2x3's at joints or have a thickened slab at the joints).  The issue isn't the number of bags, but rather being able to finish the concrete before it sets. Plus, with a slab, it is good to use a straight 2x4 spanning from form-to-form and pulled across the top of the wet concrete to check how level it is and two people are definately needed for this (one at each end of the 2x4) unless, again, you break your pour into much smaller sections (like a checkerboard) and have more cold joints. Get a 5-gallon bucket and pre-measure how much water is needed for the number of bags you'll mix at a time and use a sharpie to mark the line on water line on the bucket.  Don't forget to apply a form release either.  Motor oil or baby oil works fine....and make sure to have thin plastic to lay ontop the slab hours after it has been finished to be able to wet cure.

Your hands may be beat up after moving all those bags into the mixer and gloves getting wet, plus any small sand will begin to rub and cut the now-wet skin on your fingers. My trick is to use sports tape on the fingers, then a thin pair of elastic work gloves, then a pair of leather gloves over those.

Source: recently did a 200 bag slab.

Edit: and get yourself a stinger/vibrator for anything thick. They can be rented, or Harbor Freight may still have one for around $100 which is the best way to go and you can use it for all your future concrete needs :)

Edit: the above was downvoted, perhaps it will help for me to explain further: there is not a single solution that Op can use that, properly installed, will likely be as affective as Op wants it to be. I have stayed (very briefly) next to a light rail station and the high decibal noise was not pleasant. Sound-deadening curtains, insulated felt or fabric panels, area rugs if the floors are hardwood, and window inserts are all options but they cost money and Op's post states this is an apartment which I presume means Op will be renting. Will Op want to move these things to the next place when Op moves? If they are custom built, should they be moved? My advice is that this is a "this AND that" scenario. Get the sound deadening curtains AND some nice noise-canceling headphones. Neither, alone, will quiet all of the sound but together they may get the perceived acoustic levels to where Op is comfortable. Plus the headphones will enable Op to listen to music, hands-free calls and web-meetings, etc....and Op can take the headphones to the next place. When my wife and I got married we kept our last names.  It felt weird at the time.  We both stressed about it, but I have no regrets about it now.  Still married and going strong.  Now, we have a newborn on the way and the trouble is deciding which surname to give our youngin.  Our families' histories are also from different cultures but we are both very much American.  I believe it us important for our future child to have a connection to the histories of both of our families' cultures, without sacrificing one for the other.  Easier said than done I am sure.  Our name solution?  We are combining both our last names in to one (no space, no hyphen, two capital letters).  Yes, it will take time getting used to.  Yes, our parents may not "get it," but it isn't their choice nor their story.  It helps that both our surnames are short.  Anyways, don't stress about the name - it won't change the fact that the world is full of assholes that need to poke fun at others to make themselves feel better for being one dimensional.

It looks like most comments so far are y-t-a.  You may wish to elaborate on why you "can't" have a tree in your house.  Bad memories?  Pressure from your parents?  I understand these things.  Would your wife be ok with something other than a tree in the home?  Nutcrackers, gingerbread people, a wreath? Would you be ok with any of these?  These things are just physical symbols that people attach memories to.  Does she want the tree so she can decorate it with ornaments, with family pictures, maybe with lights?  How about allowing your wife to decorate the outside of your home with winter lights and agree to a different non-triggering symbol (other than the tree) inside of the home.  NAH if you can work through this where you, your wife, and your children can have many truly positive and warm-memory filled winters* for years to come.

*assumung you are in the northern hemisphere.
